claims.text: In the local Universe, star-forming galaxies exhibit a positive relation between stellar mass and gas-phase oxygen abundance that steepens below about 10^10.5 solar masses, flattens above that scale, and shows roughly 0.1 dex scatter.

Different strong-line and direct-electron-temperature metallicity calibrations can shift inferred gas-phase oxygen abundances by as much as about 0.7 dex, so mass–metallicity normalizations are comparable across studies only when the underlying abundance scales are matched.

In local star-forming galaxies, gas-phase metallicity is associated with star-formation rate at fixed stellar mass, and a mass–star-formation-rate–metallicity surface reduces residual scatter relative to the two-variable mass–metallicity relation.

Mean stellar metallicity increases with stellar mass among local galaxies, forming an integrated-history relation that is distinct from the gas-phase mass–metallicity relation and reflects the metallicity of stars formed over a galaxy's history.

Consistently calibrated samples show lower gas-phase oxygen abundance at fixed stellar mass toward higher redshift, with a measured decline of about 0.11 dex per unit redshift out to redshift roughly 3.3.
JWST/NIRSpec observations extend the mass–metallicity relation to low-mass galaxies at redshifts of about 4 to 10, which show lower metallicity at fixed stellar mass than local samples.

In local disc galaxies, star-forming regions follow a positive relation between local stellar surface mass density and local gas-phase metallicity that can reproduce important aspects of the global mass–metallicity relation and radial gradients.

Whether the fundamental mass–star-formation-rate–metallicity relation is redshift-invariant is contested, with some matched analyses finding no evolution out to redshift about 3.3 while other data and simulations indicate substantial offsets and an evolving secondary star-formation dependence at higher redshift.

Which metallicity scale best transfers to high redshift is unresolved, as local direct-temperature and photoionization-model calibrations disagree in absolute normalization and simulations indicate that applying some local calibrations to early galaxies can bias inferred oxygen abundance downward.

The relative roles of gas inflow, star-formation efficiency, gas fraction, and metal-loaded outflows in setting the mass–metallicity relation remain model-dependent, and an observed relation does not by itself uniquely identify a single outflow law.

Offsets between the stellar metallicities of passive and star-forming galaxies have been interpreted as favoring a prolonged reduced-inflow (starvation) phase over instantaneous gas removal, though the relative contribution of outflows and the dominant timescale remain debated.

Cosmic chemical enrichment is described as a long-term balance between pristine gas inflow, star-formation efficiency, and metal-loaded outflows, because classical closed-box models fail to reproduce the observed metallicity distribution of long-lived low-mass stars known as the G-dwarf problem.

In local spiral galaxies, gas-phase and stellar metallicities rise together at low stellar mass but decouple at high stellar mass, where present-day gas reaches an enriched equilibrium while the average stellar metallicity reflects earlier, less-enriched epochs of peak star formation.

The Type Ia supernova delay-time distribution follows a continuously declining power law of about t^-1.07 from a few hundred million years to over 10 billion years, making Type Ia supernovae the dominant source of delayed iron enrichment.

Low- and intermediate-mass stars passing through the asymptotic giant branch are major nucleosynthetic sources of carbon, secondary nitrogen, and roughly half of the elements heavier than iron produced by slow neutron capture.

The nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio in star-forming galaxies shows a flat plateau near log(N/O) of about -1.6 at low oxygen abundance, consistent with primary nitrogen from massive stars, and rises steeply at high oxygen abundance where secondary nitrogen from intermediate-mass stars dominates.
Local star-forming disc galaxies generally show negative radial gas-phase metallicity gradients, with enriched centers and metal-poorer outskirts, consistent with inside-out disc assembly.

Stellar radial migration driven by resonant interactions with transient spiral arms and central bars can flatten and blur stellar metallicity gradients over time and broaden the age–metallicity distribution at a given galactocentric radius.

Whether the [alpha/Fe] ratio is a clean star-formation-timescale clock is debated, since a top-heavy initial mass function or metallicity-dependent stellar yields could raise [alpha/Fe] independently of the star-formation history.

The JWST detection of a supersolar nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio in the galaxy GN-z11 at redshift 10.6, only about 440 million years after the Big Bang, is in tension with standard delayed nitrogen enrichment and has prompted competing explanations invoking Wolf-Rayet winds, tidal disruption events, or dense stellar clusters.

Whether high-redshift disc galaxies have steeper, flat, or inverted radial metallicity gradients is debated, as observed gradients at redshifts of about 1 to 3 are diverse and may reflect genuine cold-flow accretion and feedback or observational beam-smearing.

The progenitor channels of Type Ia supernovae remain debated, as the single-degenerate scenario readily produces prompt explosions but struggles with the late-time delay-time tail, while the double-degenerate merger scenario naturally yields the tail but has difficulty producing enough prompt events.
